The auxiliary verb and the infinitive are said in one breath: «vuelvo-a-leer», «acabo-de-llegar». The preposition “a” links up with the vowel before it.
-ando / -iendo, stressed on the second-to-last syllable: pen-SAN-do, le-YEN-do, es-cri-BIEN-do.
Two “c”s: the first [k], the second [θ] in Spain: tra-duk-THIÓN.

Learners often say “otra vez” or “de nuevo” for “again”. That’s correct, but “volver a” is much more natural: «Ha vuelto a llover» (It’s started raining again).
“Acabar de” in the imperfect = the very recent past relative to another moment: «Acababa de llegar cuando sonó el teléfono» (I had just arrived when the phone rang).

The negative of “seguir + gerund” is made with “sin + infinitive”: «Sigue sin contestar» (He still isn’t answering). The negative of “llevar”: «Llevo dos años sin fumar» (I haven’t smoked for two years).
The participle agrees with the object and shows an accumulated result:
I’ve read three chapters so far.
The difference: «He traducido veinte páginas» (a fact) versus «Tengo traducidas veinte páginas» (a result I have now, stressing the quantity).

That evening, Ecaterina didn’t go straight home. She asked Ana to come with her for a cup of tea in the institute’s café. She hadn’t told that story for forty years, she said, and if she didn’t tell it now, she never would. Ana ordered two teas, switched off her phone and sat down to listen.

In 1977, when Romania and Spain had just restored diplomatic relations, Ecaterina was thirty-two and worked as a translator at a state publishing house. She spoke Spanish better than anyone in Bucharest, though she had never been to Spain. She had taught herself, with dictionaries, borrowed novels and a radio that picked up Radio Exterior de España at night, when nobody could hear her.

One day she was called into an office at the ministry. They needed an interpreter for the new trade office in Madrid. It was a two-year post. Ecaterina almost said no, because her mother lived alone and had a heart condition. It was her own mother who persuaded her: “Go, my girl. Doors like that open once in a lifetime.”

Madrid dazzled her from the very first day. The city had just come out of forty years of dictatorship and it seemed as if everyone had started talking at once: in the bars, in the squares, in the newspapers. Ecaterina, who came from a country where you had to weigh every word, spent her afternoons sitting in cafés listening to people argue, the way you listen to music.

It was in a bookshop on the calle de las Huertas that she met Andrés. He was the bookseller, a tall, tousled man with round glasses and endless patience with customers who never bought anything. Ecaterina went in looking for a novel by Cortázar and came out three hours later with five books, a dinner invitation and the feeling that her life had just changed.

The two years became four, and the four became ten. Each time her contract was about to end, someone in Bucharest decided to extend it, because nobody translated like her. Meanwhile, Ecaterina kept translating Spanish novels into Romanian at night, in the back room of Andrés’s bookshop, surrounded by books and tobacco smoke. In those ten years she managed to translate fourteen books.

Ecaterina remembered one night above all: 23 February 1981. They were in the bookshop when, suddenly, the radio interrupted the music. Armed civil guards had just stormed into the Congress of Deputies. Nobody knew what was going to happen. Andrés pulled down the shutter, switched off the lights, and they sat on the floor of the back room, among the books, listening to the radio until six in the morning.

“I came from a country where that sort of thing could last forty years,” Ecaterina told Ana. “I was trembling. Andrés didn’t stop talking to me all night, about books, about poets, about silly things, so that I wouldn’t think. When the king spoke on television in the morning and it was all over, Andrés started crying like a child. It was the first time I saw him cry. That morning I knew I loved him.”

Andrés asked her to marry him twice. The first time in 1981, on the terrace of a bar in the Plaza de Santa Ana. The second time in 1985, in front of the poetry shelves. Both times Ecaterina said not yet. She couldn’t explain to him what marrying a foreigner meant for a Romanian civil servant in those days: that she would have to choose between him and her mother, and that if she chose wrongly, she would never see either of them again.

In September 1987 a telegram arrived. Her mother had had a heart attack. Ecaterina had to go back immediately. They gave her two days to arrange the journey. She spent the first night packing and the second in front of the closed door of the bookshop, at three in the morning, with a letter in her hand that she had started ten times.

She never posted it. She was afraid that if she said goodbye to him, she wouldn’t be able to get on the plane. And she was afraid, too, that someone from the office would see her. So she left. One autumn day, early in the morning, without saying goodbye, with the letter in her coat pocket.

Her mother lived another six years. Ecaterina looked after her until the end. After 1989, when people could finally write freely, she sent three letters to the bookshop on the calle de las Huertas. None of them got a reply. In 1995 a colleague who travelled to Madrid told her the bookshop had closed and nobody knew where the bookseller had gone.

The first years in Bucharest were the hardest. Ecaterina worked at the publishing house by day and looked after her mother at night. Sometimes, when her mother finally fell asleep, she would sit in the kitchen with a Spanish book and start translating in a whisper, just to hear that language again. She no longer spoke it with anyone. It was as if she had left part of herself in the back room of a bookshop in Madrid.

Ecaterina kept on translating. She became one of the best translators of Spanish literature in the country. But she stopped going to Madrid. She was invited many times to conferences, book launches, prize ceremonies. She always found an excuse. She said a city where you have been so happy is dangerous: if you go back, you may discover that happiness wasn’t waiting for you.

Ana had gone an hour without touching her tea, which had gone cold. Ecaterina took an old, yellowed envelope with worn edges out of her bag. It was the letter. The one she never managed to post. She had kept it for forty years in the same coat, then in a box, then in the drawer of her bedside table.

“And now,” said Ecaterina very quietly, “a publisher is asking me to translate the first novel by a young author I don’t know. A novel set in a bookshop on the calle de las Huertas. And dedicated to a woman who left one autumn day in 1987 without saying goodbye.”

Ana took the envelope carefully. It wasn’t sealed. Ecaterina signalled to her not to open it. “Not yet,” she said. “I haven’t read it for forty years. I can wait a little longer.” Ana gave it back, and Ecaterina put it back in her bag, slowly, like someone putting away something that is still alive.
“I don’t think anything,” Ecaterina interrupted. “At my age, I’ve stopped believing in coincidences. But I’ve also stopped believing they don’t exist.”

Before saying goodbye, Ecaterina asked Ana a favour. She wanted her to help look for something about the author on the internet, because she still didn’t understand how those things worked. Ana promised to do it that same evening. On the metro on the way home, she opened the browser on her phone and typed the name: Marta Gil.

There was a photo. A woman of about thirty-five, with short hair and round glasses, smiling in front of a shelf full of books. Underneath, a short biography: “Marta Gil was born in Madrid in 1990. She grew up among the books of her grandfather’s bookshop, in the Barrio de las Letras. This is her first novel.”

Ana looked at the photo for a long time. The round glasses. The bookshelf. The Barrio de las Letras, where the calle de las Huertas was. She almost called Ecaterina straight away. Then she looked at the clock: it was eleven at night. She decided to wait until the next day.

When she got home, Mihai was in the kitchen, practising the tortilla with Carmen’s frying pan. Ana showed him the photo without saying anything. Mihai looked at it, then at Ana, and turned off the heat. “Are you going to tell her?” he asked. Ana said she didn’t know. That sometimes a question can do more harm than silence. Mihai, who had often seen families waiting for news in the hospital corridor, replied that silence hurts too, only more slowly.

She couldn’t sleep. At two in the morning she was still looking at the photo on her phone, while Mihai snored softly beside her. She thought about Ion Mărgărit, who had left without saying goodbye to his friends. She thought about Vasile and Ileana. She thought that in her new Romanian life she had learnt something she had never known in Madrid: that stories left unfinished don’t disappear. They wait, sometimes for forty years, for someone to open them again.

At seven in the morning, just as she was finally about to fall asleep, her phone rang. It was a message from Ecaterina, full of spelling mistakes, because she still hadn’t learnt to use the keyboard properly: “Ana. I’ve reread the dedication. At the end there’s something I didn’t see. A small letter. Come as soon as you can.”
